title: Scale-free wave localization at topological multicriticality
authors: Zhijie Xue, Yuan Tian, Nanyu Chen, Xiujuan Zhang, Tao Li, Shuang Zhang, Fuxin Guan
abstract: Spatial wave localization at boundaries is conventionally restricted to exponential decay. Here, we observe a scale-free boundary mode exhibiting anomalous polynomial decay, highlighted by strictly linear spatial envelopes, driven by topological multicriticality in acoustic metamaterials. We establish a universal geometric bulk-boundary correspondence rooted in singularity theory by mapping n-th order topological multicriticality onto Arnold An catastrophe. We prove that defectiveness in the spatial transfer matrix enforces a (n-1)-th power spatial decay of boundary modes. At a topological tri-critical point, the singularity of winding function manifests as an A2 fold catastrophe. This dictates a strictly linear spatial decay, marking a sharp departure from the conventional exponential scaling paradigm. Using acoustic metamaterial platforms tuned to a tricritical point, we experimentally demonstrate this linear decay envelope in 1D, and further generalize it to two-dimensional systems to realize scale-free corner modes with simultaneous linear decay along orthogonal directions. While existing critical topology frameworks rely on entanglement spectra to diagnose mode existence in gapless regimes, our work bridges catastrophe theory with topological matter at multicriticalities, advancing the field from abstract mode identification to deterministic real-space wavefunction engineering.
summary: This research reveals that at specific topological multicritical points, wave localization at boundaries does not decay exponentially but instead follows a universal, scale-free polynomial decay dictated by the underlying singularity structure. By mapping this physics onto Arnold's catastrophe theory, the authors provide a deterministic framework for engineering these anomalous boundary modes, which they experimentally confirm in acoustic metamaterials.
main_problem: The paper investigates anomalous wave localization at boundaries, challenging the conventional understanding that wave decay must be exponential.
main_result: They establish that at topological multicriticalities, boundary modes exhibit anomalous polynomial decay, which is mathematically linked to the system's singularity structure via catastrophe theory.
method: The study combines theoretical analysis using transfer matrices and singularity theory (Arnold's catastrophe) with experimental realization using acoustic metamaterials.
model_or_system: The primary model involves acoustic metamaterials, mathematically described using an open boundary condition (OBC) Hamiltonian and a transfer matrix approach, which is generalized to 2D lattices.
key_observables: Anomalous polynomial decay of boundary modes ($\propto (N_A-j)^{n-1}$), topological winding numbers, and the observation of specific band touching types (quadratic vs. linear).
important_parameters: Topological multicriticalities, the order of the singularity ($n$), and the parameters defining the phase diagram (e.g., $t_0, t_1, t_2$).
main_assumptions: The work assumes that the geometric structure of the bulk-boundary correspondence can be universally mapped onto Arnold's catastrophe theory framework.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the schematic of the OBC Hamiltonian, canonical unfolding geometries for various catastrophes (fold, cusp, etc.), the topological phase diagram, and spatial profiles confirming linear/polynomial decay in 1D and 2D.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the mathematical link between defective transfer matrices and polynomial decay, then mapping this to catastrophe theory, and finally demonstrating this universal scaling law both numerically and experimentally in acoustic metamaterials.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, universal mathematical tool (catastrophe theory) to predict and engineer non-standard wave localization behaviors in topological matter, bridging abstract mathematics with concrete physical realization in metamaterials.
